extracted.intended_audience: scientists (especially those affiliated with ESA/Hubble) preparing press releases or working with institutional Public Information Officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientists on preparing press releases about research results, including newsworthiness criteria, visual support, collaboration with PIOs, and practical science-writing advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor style, level and content to the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Always tailor the style, level and content of a press release to suit the needs of the press and not the secondary target groups (decision-makers, mediators, scientists, public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases primarily target journalists; adapt vocabulary, technical detail, and angle for newsrooms rather than for specialist audiences or the general public's peripheral stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate closely with the scientist/Principal Investigator
rubrics_metrics.description: Close collaboration with the scientist (the Principal Investigator) is vital: they can supply a short plain-language text or explain the result over the phone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should be prepared to spend time explaining the science, provide accurate details and help create correct imagery. Their approval is required before release.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIO co-operation in drafting and institutional review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Public Information Officer co-operates with the scientist to draft the press release; after scientist approval it is often sent to an internal editorial board that reviews political and scientific issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect iterative drafting with PIO involvement and possible internal review for institutional/policy considerations; plan timelines accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release main goals
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release should aim to (1) increase awareness of science and the scientific work process, (2) increase awareness of the organisation, and (3) increase awareness of specific scientific projects, instruments or missions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three goals to choose the release's angle and to measure its success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different types of press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three significant types: News release (focuses on discoveries), Photo release (contains images but no big discovery), and Video release (Video News Release for broadcast or web).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the format that fits the content; many written releases are accompanied by high-quality photos and video. VNRs translate print into the sound-and-picture format needed by TV/web broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual support is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Images, illustrations and visual design are key factors in successful science communication; without good visuals the chances of 'selling' the story diminish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with communicators to create artist's impressions or videos based on raw data; invest effort in high-quality, eye-catching visuals because they significantly increase media uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is 'news' (the event has just taken place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fresh results/events; coordinate release timing with publication or events to maximize news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: An issue that has direct or near-direct influence on people’s lives such as fatalities and material damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize aspects of the result that affect public safety, health, economy or daily life when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: The story has local appeal or local interest (happened in the town or the country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, highlight local connections (institutions, scientists, locations) to increase regional media interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Implications
rubrics_metrics.description: A result that has profound consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame and explain long-term or far-reaching implications clearly if the finding genuinely alters understanding or application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Settles a controversial debate or a much-debated topic that contains intrigues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If research resolves controversy or fuels debate, present the context and stakes to enhance news value while being careful with claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal or quirky angle (e.g., 'Astronomer discovers new galaxies while raising three children...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human stories or unusual personal details to make complex science relatable, but avoid sensationalism that misrepresents the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: A mysterious phenomenon, quirky details, an unexpected result or a chance discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight genuine surprises or puzzles in the findings to attract curiosity; do not overstate uncertainty as mystery when it is well understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Major science
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents a major discovery of a new phenomenon or class of object or an incremental gain in knowledge about a principal field of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state what is novel and why it matters within the field; quantify or qualify the advance relative to prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — New interesting angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Twisting an old result in a new way, such as a new, better image that confirms a known result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novelty is in the perspective or improved data (e.g., better image), explain how this adds value beyond previous reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — A record
rubrics_metrics.description: First, largest, most distant, fastest, oldest …
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applicable, emphasize 'record' attributes (first/most/etc.) and provide context and verification for such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — 'Sexy' topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Some topics almost always capture public attention (e.g., Solar System topics, space weather, black holes, extrasolar planets, extraterrestrial life, human spaceflight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that 'sexy' topics draw quick headlines but ensure scientific accuracy and avoid hype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional beauty of an image can be newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visually striking imagery as a legitimate angle; pair aesthetic appeal with explanatory context to avoid shallow coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Publication in distinguished journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Results published in, for example, Nature or Science tend to attract more interest from journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate embargoes and citations with journal publication and mention the outlet to increase credibility and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Crosslinking (piggybacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letting a result piggyback on another news story in a related, parallel or even remotely related field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify connections to contemporaneous stories to broaden relevance; explicitly state links so journalists can see the angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-or-Not checklist (use news criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think you have a good science result, check the News Criteria list to see if your result is likely to interest the press and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the news criteria as a screening tool before proposing a press release; if multiple criteria are met, pursue the release proactively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be proactive in alerting PIOs
rubrics_metrics.description: If your science fulfils one or more news criteria, do not hesitate to tell the communications office; they can help publicize the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely notification allows PIOs to prepare visuals, coordinate co-releases, and plan media engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with the communications office to prepare the press release and be prepared to spend time explaining the science and making information available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in drafting, provide clarifications, supply data and imagery, and review drafts promptly to meet deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve other institutions for coordinated/co-release
rubrics_metrics.description: The PIO will interface with PIOs of other institutions involved, possibly proposing a simultaneous co-release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate messaging and timing across partner institutions to maximize reach and avoid conflicting statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create eye-catching images (practically mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sort of eye-catching image or illustration to accompany the press release is practically mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with communicators to create appealing and scientifically correct imagery; images substantially improve pick-up by media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add value via specialized webpages and extra materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists may create specialised webpages with additional information, translations, more images, graphs, technical movies, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide supplementary material for journalists and the public; scientists often have better local media contacts and can supply in-depth content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare properly (set boundary conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set boundary conditions regarding topic, length, target group and style before writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the intended audience and constraints early to keep the release focused and appropriately pitched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your research (answer the six golden questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by answering: What? When? Where? Who? Why? and How? Also scan literature, review your own writing, and mine the web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish factual context and prior work; collecting background prevents errors and helps writers craft accurate, contextualized copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure your thinking (brainstorm and find angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise ideas and look for patterns or connections that help choose an effective angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorming can reveal compelling narratives or linkages that clarify the story for non-specialist readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relax during initial drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow oneself to relax and not be overly concerned about the reader in early drafts to sound genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a relaxed first draft phase, then refocus on clarity and audience in editing stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent (follow a style guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow consistent writing guidelines (organisational style guide or personal standard) for spelling, grammar, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency improves professionalism and avoids distracting errors; spellings and grammar should match organisational norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify — make text as simple as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Make texts as simple as possible because readers do not have time for lengthy explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language, short sentences, and avoid unnecessary jargon; preserve accuracy while maximising accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain — assume the reader knows nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Match writing to target group level, always spell out abbreviations, build explanations from the lowest level without patronising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough background for non-experts, define terms, and avoid unexplained acronyms; balance clarity with respect for readers' intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit and seek external editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-reading and editing always improves quality; especially effective if the editor is someone other than the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for multiple revisions and independent review to catch errors, unclear phrasing, or misleading claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern aids (spellcheckers, thesauruses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilise features in word processors like spellcheckers and thesauruses to aid writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools speed minor corrections but do not replace substantive editing and expert review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompany written releases with high-quality photos and video when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases any written release will be accompanied by high-quality photos and a video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple media formats (images, video clips) to suit different outlets; ensure correct captions, crediting and metadata for media use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect institutional involvement and approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically the institution is involved either through its scientists or a project managed by the institution, and institutional approval processes apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for institutional sign-off, checks on political/sensitivity issues, and coordination with other stakeholders before publication.
